headline: First edition of the migration tab. Pressure from Belarus is concentrated on Latvia, where attempted illegal crossings in 2026 already exceed the whole of 2025, and Latvia wants to keep its special border regime until mid-2027. On the EU side, the Baltic states are formally classed as at risk and cannot be made to accept relocated migrants; no transfers of migrants to the Baltic states from other EU countries have been reported.
pressure_note: Latvia's border guard says 12,857 people were stopped trying to cross from Belarus by 10 November, above the 12,046 for all of 2025; recent daily figures are in the tens. Smugglers, tunnels and damage to border equipment continue. Lithuania and Poland see far fewer attempts, and Estonia closes its road crossings with Russia on 1 December.
eu_note: Under the EU Migration Pact each country chooses whether to take people, pay or send other support; Latvia and Lithuania say they will not take relocated migrants, and Estonia may ask to have its share reduced. The 2027 round is being negotiated after the Commission's 6 November report. Germany is resuming returns under EU rules to Italy and Greece, not the Baltic states.
changed: First edition, so there is no earlier day to compare with. Counts cover items reported between 10 and 17 November; from tomorrow they cover only what is new since the previous edition.
bottom_line: The evidence points to two different kinds of risk. The immediate one is pressure organised from Belarus: Latvian prosecutors describe smuggling networks, payments of about 5,000 dollars a crossing, migrants pushed to damage border equipment and suspected involvement of Belarusian border officials, which fits the hybrid pressure described in Lithuania's 2026 threat assessment. The second, which many people fear, is that other EU countries will shift their migrants onto the Baltic states. Under current rules that is limited: relocation is voluntary in practice, fewer than 1,000 people are expected to be physically relocated across the whole EU in 2026, and the Baltic states have declined to take any. The lawful channel that could grow is returns of people who first entered the EU through Latvia or Lithuania and moved on west; Poland already checks its border with Lithuania until March 2027 and turns people back. Claims that the EU forces the Baltic states to take thousands of migrants are not supported by the rules or the numbers. Daily crossing numbers swing widely and are published unevenly, so single days say little.

headline: Lithuania moves to take no relocated migrants under the EU solidarity scheme and pay instead, replacing a May pledge to take 58 from Cyprus; in Estonia, parties argue over checks on the Latvian border. No new organised crossing incidents or transfers of migrants to the Baltic states were reported.
pressure_note: No new daily crossing figures were found since the previous edition. The latest: Latvia stopped 12,857 attempts by 10 November; Lithuania turned back 1,896 people by 7 November, already more than the 1,652 in all of 2025; Poland recorded 482 attempts by 8 November and plans to extend its Belarus border buffer zone to 27 February 2027, citing drones and balloons. Belarus also ordered a snap readiness check of its border-guard units.
eu_note: A Lithuanian government commission approved the interior minister's proposal to take no relocated migrants and pay into the EU solidarity pool instead; the government still has to approve it and the amount is not yet known. The Pact allows this choice. Five EU states announced a Rwanda return hub for rejected asylum seekers, which Estonia supports but will not join; it does not change Baltic obligations. No transfers to the Baltic states were reported.
changed: The migration pressure score is unchanged at 12 of 30, with no rating changes; trends move from New to Unchanged. All five counts are 0 (yesterday: organised incidents 1, new border measures 2, misleading claims 2). New since yesterday: Lithuania's plan to pay instead of relocating anyone; the Estonian party debate on checks at the Latvian border; the Rwanda return hub. Catching up: Poland's draft to extend its Belarus buffer zone (14 November) and Lithuania's year-to-date figure. Correction: yesterday's edition said the Baltic states have declined to take any relocated migrants; in fact Lithuania agreed in May to take 58 from Cyprus, a choice it is now moving to replace with a payment.
bottom_line: Today's news mostly concerns how the Baltic states use the choices the EU rules give them, not anything imposed on them. Lithuania's move to pay rather than relocate shows that the solidarity scheme lets a country refuse relocation entirely, which again contradicts claims that the EU forces the Baltic states to take migrants; it also shows that Lithuania had earlier volunteered to take a small group, so the picture is a national choice, not a refusal from the start. The organised pressure from Belarus continues on the evidence of recent weeks, with Latvia most affected and Lithuania's own turn-backs now above last year's total, although no fresh daily figures were published in this window. The Estonian debate on checks at the Latvian border is about onward movement inside Schengen and is partly driven by opposition parties; the government is not proposing checks. No other EU country has been reported planning to send migrants to the Baltic states; lawful returns between EU states remain a separate and, for now, quiet channel.
